w1l1: Business pressures come from both inside and outside a firm. An organisation has some control over its internal environment, but very little over external conditions.

The lecture identifies four pressures: shorter product lives, higher customer expectations, high uncertainty and global impact. Treat them as reasons to innovate rather than conditions a firm can simply switch off.
Innovation is the response to these pressures, not a substitute for recognising them. The next topics explain each pressure and its examples.
Why product lives are getting shorter
A product life cycle has four phases: introduction, growth, maturity and decline. A shorter cycle leaves less time to develop and recover value from an offering.
The lecture compares earlier consumer-durable lives of 10-20 years with 2-3 years. These are the course examples, not a current lifespan guarantee for every product.

Television moves from black-and-white to colour, flat screens and later display technologies. The mobile-phone example begins with bulky phones in India in 1996 and shows rapid replacement by newer devices.
Customers want low cost, high quality and fast delivery together. Do not treat these as alternatives where delivering one excuses missing the others.
Online comparisons across Amazon, Flipkart and eBay make competing offers easier to compare. This raises expectations for the whole experience.

Heterogeneity means customer groups differ in their needs and expectations. The lecture illustrates this through forms that add transgender and undisclosed options rather than assuming only two categories.
Kedarnath and Delhi smog illustrate uncertainty: vulnerable locations and debated causes make outcomes difficult to predict. Preparing for uncertainty differs from assuming it can be eliminated.
Global impact means a local event can affect an international business chain. Apple is the lecture example: US design, Chinese manufacturing and worldwide markets are connected.
A firm therefore needs to consider events outside its own premises and country. Internal operational control does not remove exposure to external disruption.
From industrial scale to new value
The development sequence is Europe, North America, Japan and China. The lecture links them respectively with industrialisation, economic power, quality and low-cost manufacturing.
Europe used colonies as markets; North America emphasised scale. Japan showed that removing waste could improve quality while lowering cost, whereas China became the cost benchmark.
Matching an existing benchmark is not the whole answer. Innovation must reach products, processes, customer experience and business models across the organisation.

The course uses Ola and Uber without owned taxis, Alibaba without held inventory, and free digital services to question familiar ways of earning revenue. These are lecture-era illustrations of a business model, not a claim that every firm has the same structure today.
Commercialisation turns an innovation into use and value. That can support jobs and economic growth, beyond producing an interesting idea.
Keep the four business pressures together: shrinking product lives, rising expectations, uncertainty and global impact. They explain why organisations need continuing innovation.
w1l2: Drucker calls innovation the specific tool of entrepreneurs. It lets them exploit change as an opportunity for a different business or service.
The defining word is innovation, not design, marketing or communication. Those activities can support the work, but they do not fill the blank in this quotation.
The lecture links changes to opportunities: sanitation to waste services, corruption to IT transparency, GST to compliance software and demonetisation to e-payments.
The three important I's are **Idea, Implementation and Impact**. Integration and Industry are the look-alike options, not members of this list.
**Idea + Implementation = Invention. Invention + Impact = Innovation.** A working result alone is not enough to complete the second equation.
If the question asks what the sum gives, the answer is innovation. Design, marketing, communication and management do not replace the final term.
An invention may remain in a laboratory or file without creating impact. To call it innovation, connect the implemented idea to actual use and value.
Impact depends on the organisation: a business may look at market share, cost or profit; a school at higher study; a religious body at people giving up addictions.
At the idea stage, keep an open mind and postpone judgment. Screening too soon can stop an idea before implementation and its potential impact can be explored.
Novel implementation of an existing idea
An idea need not be entirely new for its implementation to be innovative. Gandhi's use of non-violence is the lecture example.
Non-violence already had roots in Jainism and Buddhism. The novelty lay in applying it as a mass movement rather than claiming the original idea was newly invented.
Separate the age of the idea from the way it is put into use. The course equation still requires implementation and impact, not novelty in the idea alone.
Innovation begins with curiosity: asking why, how and what if. The statement that it is always a smooth linear process is false.
Experiments, failures and restarts make the process iterative. Each iteration can add cost and delay market entry, so immediate profit from an idea should not be assumed.
Innovation involves both risk and mitigation, and it is a team activity. Reducing potential losses differs from pretending there is no risk or expecting a lone genius to do everything.
w1l3: The lecture separates resistance to change from difficulty predicting the future. Resistance is not wanting to change; prediction disability is not being able to see what comes next.
Ignoring an idea, fear of failure, inertia and low confidence are forms of resistance. A boss dismissing a junior or parents dismissing a career wish illustrate ignoring an idea.

For the quiz, select ignoring the idea and inertia. Ignoring the chances of failure is overlooking risk, while exuding confidence is not resistance; a mentor can help turn low confidence into willingness to try.
VUCA expands to Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity and Ambiguity. Knowing the four words is different from treating their meanings as interchangeable.

Volatility is unstable change of unknown duration, illustrated by demonetisation and GST rollout. Under uncertainty, cause and effect are known but change remains possible. Complexity is different again: many interconnected parts make information difficult to organise, even when the parts are known.
Ambiguity means no precedent or an unknown relationship: **unknown unknowns**. A new market or a product outside core competence illustrates this; the quiz's unknown-unknowns answer is ambiguity.
Emotion and analysis must work together
The elephant represents the emotional, intuitive system; the rider represents deliberate analysis. The elephant has power, while the rider can look ahead but cannot direct change effectively alone.

At night the analytical rider sets an alarm, but in the morning the emotional elephant switches it off. The route story similarly contrasts an attractive unfamiliar path with a familiar but dangerous one.
Change needs harmony between the two systems, not analysis alone. Learning to drive illustrates how deliberate actions can become intuitive with practice.
w1l4: Ad hoc fixes and systematic innovation
Jugaad refers to an ad hoc fix in the lecture's North Indian example. It addresses an immediate need but is contrasted with a planned, sustainable innovation process.
Systematic innovation follows a deliberate path rather than relying on a one-off workaround. The lecture links it with intellectual property and intellectual property rights.
IP can then be commercialised or transferred as technology. Keep the planned route separate from the temporary nature of the jugaad comparison.

Breakthrough innovations create a new level: the course examples are fire, the wheel, the steam engine and the shift from landline to mobile. Select the first three when the quiz lists them against 2G-to-3G.

Incremental innovation improves what already exists. Kaizen reduces waste, rework and scrap; moving from 2G to 3G to 4G is the incremental example, not a new-to-the-world breakthrough. Week 5 uses a more detailed classification and calls 3G-to-4G generational. Use the framework named in the question; neither example is a new-to-the-world breakthrough.

The types work together: a breakthrough is followed by adaptations and improvements before another breakthrough. Incremental changes inside a firm can be important even when outsiders do not notice them.
Frugal innovation treats resource constraints as an opportunity rather than a liability. It aims for good quality and the greatest customer value at the lowest cost.
It does not aim to wow customers with technically sophisticated products. In the quiz, both the constraint-as-opportunity statement and the low-cost, good-quality statement are true.
Understanding what customers value prevents marketing myopia. Co-creation helps shape that value, and frugal solutions often serve people whose needs existing offers do not meet.
The four areas are product, process, customer experience and business model. Product examples include iPhone, iPad, smartwatches and smart glasses.

Process examples include Six Sigma, Lean, TQM and Kanban; these can be internal, incremental and invisible outside the firm. Tracking deliveries or visas and birthday reminders change customer experience instead.

Business-model innovation is the most encompassing area. IPL combines a franchise model, T20 product, changed rules as process, and entertainment as customer experience, so an example can involve more than one area.
w1l5: The lecture contrasts emotions, which are hard to teach directly, with analysis, which can be taught. Awareness, confidence and removal of myths help people approach innovation.
Framing matters: a positive goal such as removing polio is different from merely avoiding illness. Awareness should make the desired change understandable.
The three schools introduced here are design thinking, systems thinking and lateral thinking. Learn each school's focus before comparing their examples.
Design thinking is **human-centered, solution-focused and action-oriented**. The incorrect quiz description is product-centered: people, not the product alone, are the starting point.

Empathy covers behaviour, emotions, anxieties and aspirations. Cross-functional teams connect quality, cost, delivery and features, while prototypes such as 3D-printed models enable fast feedback and revision.

The demonetisation example involves feedback, changing rules and several agencies; the Rs 4,000 exchange limit is a historical lecture detail that later changed. The general lesson is iterative work toward a preferred future, not a fixed policy recommendation.
Systems thinking looks for a leverage point where one change can improve the wider system. The lecture calls this a silver bullet rather than treating every symptom separately.
Peter Senge is associated with The Fifth Discipline, and Eliyahu Goldratt with the Theory of Constraints. Keep these author-concept pairings together.
The constraint cycle is to identify a constraint, fix it and then look for the next constraint. Solving one bottleneck does not mean the whole system can never face another.
Lateral thinking uses a known idea in an unrelated context. The novelty lies in the transfer rather than assuming the source idea was invented again.
The lecture applies the football franchise model to cricket through IPL. It also uses European waste-management methods in India as a transfer example.
Distinguish this from design thinking's human-centered focus and systems thinking's leverage point. The question is which way of thinking explains moving an idea across contexts.
White is information; black is barriers; red is feelings and intuition. These are perspectives for examining an issue, not labels for different products.
Yellow is values and benefits; green is creativity and new ideas; blue manages the thinking process. Keep all six mappings intact when answering the matching question.

Black and yellow are easy to reverse: black asks about barriers, yellow about benefits. Design, systems and lateral thinking remain distinct schools even when a team uses the hats to explore an issue.
w2l1: Individual barriers: motivation, roles and fear

Innovation challenges operate at two levels: the individual and the organisation. At the individual level, the list is lack of motivation, unclear roles, fear of failure and a status-quo or chalta-hai attitude.

The Maslow discussion links motivation to higher needs, with few people reaching the top two levels. Role clarity is a separate issue: having many roles does not mean knowing exactly what contribution is expected.
The marks example shows someone unhappy with 90% because a classmate has 94%. Fear and comparison can discourage trying, rather than helping people learn from an experiment.

Organisational barriers include employees not being empowered, no innovation strategy, concentration in one functional group and a lack of collaboration. Workers' participation in management and TQM appear in the empowerment discussion.

A lack of diversity, recognition and internal heroes also blocks innovation, as can complacency about successful existing offerings. The lecture contrasts collaboration through a T20 example with its absence through a Test-match example.
The Six Hats comparison explains diversity: a group wearing only one colour misses other perspectives. These are system-level conditions, not another name for an individual's fear of failure.

Internal heroes make innovative effort visible, for example through an employee-of-the-month board or photograph. Recognition is an organisational practice, not merely an employee's personal motivation.
Losing connection with customers and using the wrong measures are further organisational barriers. Measure the effort invested in innovation rather than looking only at final output.
For classification questions, internal heroes, recognition and innovation strategy belong to the organisation. Fear of failure and role clarity belong to the individual level.
w2l2: Innovation needs deliberate management, not only serendipity. The lecture's 97% Fortune 500 figure supports the importance of new ideas; it is a course statistic, not a newly measured survey.

The sequence is **collect ideas, select an idea, experiment, develop the business model, then diffusion and impact**. For the missing middle steps, X is selection, Y is experimentation and Z is business-model development.
Brainstorming, designing, validation and beta version may sound relevant to innovation, but they are not the named stages in this five-step question. Answer with the course's exact sequence.
Collect first, then select and experiment
Collection prioritises quantity and postpones judgment of quality. The idea bank deliberately contains ideas of varied quality rather than only ideas already approved.
Selection uses criteria chosen by the organisation. A prototype may help before selecting an idea, so collection and selection are not identical activities.
Experimentation tests how an idea might work. The lecture's Faraday illustration treats unsuccessful attempts as learning about ways that do not work, not as a reason to stop after one attempt.
The three Ps are **People, Planet and Profit**. They correspond to social, environmental and economic sustainability respectively.
Product, Participation and Process are the look-alike options, not substitutes for those three Ps. Learn both the words and their associated dimensions.
The lecture links CSR under the Companies Act to social sustainability. Keep this course example with People rather than treating CSR as an extra fourth P.
w2l3: An organisation may be unreceptive to ideas or not know where useful ideas come from. An idea-management system addresses resistance to change and prediction disability.
Its three key processes are idea management, buzz creation, and training and development. Buzz creation includes rewards, campaigns and awareness.
Recreation and vendor management are not the named key processes in this framework. Do not confuse a generally useful business activity with an item in the course list.
Who submits, selects and funds ideas
Idea management asks three different questions: who submits ideas, who selects them, and who funds them. Keeping the roles distinct helps turn suggestions into managed work.
Submissions can come from employees, vendors and others. Selection may involve internal experts, external experts or a mixed group.
The source of an idea is therefore not automatically the person who approves or funds it. An idea-management system needs the three responsibilities to be considered separately.
A challenge book helps develop the idea bank by identifying the right problem first. It is a way to direct idea generation, not another name for the final selected solution.
The lecture attributes the line about difficult challenges bringing innovative solutions to **Ratan Tata**. Keep the speaker with the challenge-book discussion.
Musk, Lockwood and Drucker are the distractors for that attribution. Drucker's entrepreneur-and-innovation definition is a different quotation.
Feel the pain and sense the wave
The three sources are feel the pain, sense the wave and see the waste. Begin by identifying which kind of situation the question describes.
Feel the pain means understanding difficulties experienced by current or future customers, employees and partners. Customers seeking high quality at low cost fit this source.
Sense the wave means noticing technological, demographic, regulatory or fashion changes. It is about a changing environment, not only a current complaint or unused resource.
See the waste: match the situation
See the waste looks for wasted human effort, natural resources and technological resources. Energy, water, air and land are listed resource examples; money and food are also mentioned.
A power-generation question about wasted resources belongs here. A demand for quality and low cost belongs to feel the pain, while a technology or regulation shift belongs to sense the wave.
Keep the three lists apart: processes are idea management, buzz and training; sources are pain, wave and waste; responsibilities are submit, select and fund.
w2l4: Divergent thinking explores many possible solutions and creative ideas. Convergent thinking narrows alternatives toward one solution.

Applying rules and logic to deduce the correct answer to a standard question describes convergence, not divergence. These are the misleading descriptions to reject when asked about divergent thinking.

J. P. Guilford is associated with divergent production in the 1950s. The assignment key accepts the definition in option A only, but that does not establish its Guilford attribution option as historically false. Learn the many-versus-one distinction and keep this key ambiguity in mind.
Daniel Kahneman wrote **Thinking, Fast and Slow**. His System 1 is fast and automatic; System 2 is slow and deliberate.
This is a different pair from divergent and convergent thinking. Speed and automaticity do not by themselves tell you whether someone is generating many possibilities or narrowing to one.
When matching the systems, use fast/automatic for System 1 and slow/deliberate for System 2. Keep these labels together rather than reversing their numbers.
The lecture identifies opportunities in energy, waste, health, education, IT, consumer goods and transportation. Innovation is not restricted to a single manufacturing sector.
Pricing examples include charging for tyres by usage and relating an insurance premium to health upkeep. They change how value is paid for rather than simply adding a physical feature.

Energy examples include printed solar cells and sea waves; the health discussion mentions allopathy, ayurveda and homeopathy. Treat these as lecture examples, not evidence that every approach has the same medical effectiveness.
A transition can be interesting, testing, difficult and hopeful at the same time. The fifth property in the lecture is that it incurs cost.
Change may be managed deliberately or merely passed through. If no one manages it, the lecture warns that change can end up managing the organisation.
The cost and difficulty of transition do not mean innovation should stop. They explain why moving from an idea to a changed way of working needs management.
w2l5: The lecture connects intent and its realisation with organising for that intent. Design thinking brings sequence, harmony and rhythm rather than leaving actions disconnected.
Connect means involving stakeholders with empathy. Reflexivity is central to the discussion, not merely a research method added at the end.
The aim is self-propelled productivity and growth. Keep intent, organising, connection and reflexivity together when reviewing this lecture's keywords.
Jamshedji Tata: connecting needs and enterprise
The Tata example moves from Manchester mills to a mill in Maharashtra. A crèche for working mothers connects the industrial activity to a stakeholder need.
The wider examples include steel, power, education and chemicals. The lesson is to see enterprise and supporting needs together rather than isolating one product.
Do not confuse Jamshedji Tata's industrial examples here with Ratan Tata's challenge-and-innovation quotation in the idea-management lesson.

Pencils, robots, hospitals and ships all depend on work done by other people and organisations. The pencil example refers to more than 500 companies and materials such as graphite and wood from many places.
The institutional-development discussion criticises a bankruptcy of thoughts. It asks learners to consider new possibilities rather than assuming existing institutions exhaust them.

Pine needles, Himalayan forest fires and an energy idea form the final example: a problem can become a starting point for opportunity. Keep the problem-to-idea connection rather than memorising those three words as unrelated facts.
w3l1: The lecture uses Taleb's call to learn to fail with pride, comfort and pleasure. The aim remains success, but fear of failure can stop the experiments needed to reach it.
Vivekananda's fall-and-rise example and the Gita's balance in success and failure reinforce the same mindset. An unfavourable result does not have to end the work.
The course names **learning** as the outcome of an experiment, rather than simply success or failure. A test need not give the desired result to teach something useful.
The four assumptions an experiment tests
An experiment is a planned activity that validates one or more assumptions. The four types are need, technical, production and commercial assumptions.

For paid email: need asks whether customers want it despite free alternatives; technical asks about security expertise; production asks about enough servers and 24x7 availability; commercial asks about revenue or profit.

For a child-safe social app: demand is need, child-psychology and social-media expertise are technical, Android/iOS versions are production, and parents' willingness to pay is commercial. Match the issue, not just the product name.
Low-cost testing and the failure fallacy

Low-cost experiments make repeated attempts easier and support a cost-competitive result. Designing a low-cost experiment is important for validating assumptions; getting the desired result every time is not required. Rapid prototyping, 3D printing and simulation are ways the lecture proposes to lower testing cost.
The Faraday story illustrates learning from many unsuccessful experiments. The main hindrance is **failure fallacy**: interpreting a failed test as proof the whole idea has failed.

A low-cost setup is not that hindrance. The paid-email example can be reconsidered as confidential mail like registered post, showing how learning may lead to a revised proposition rather than immediate abandonment.
w3l2: An idea champion opens channels for an idea, builds support and overcomes resistance. The champion can be a senior manager or customer and need not be the original idea giver.

The lecture compares public power to the elephant and the champion to the rider shaping its path. Gandhi championing non-violence and George Fernandes helping a stalled rail-cum-road bridge are examples.
All three roles count: build support, overcome resistance and make the idea sticky. Schumpeter's main villain in diffusion is resistance to change, distinct from failure fallacy in experimentation.
A sticky idea stays with its audience. The three Cs are **Concrete, Curiosity and Credibility**; Concern is the distractor, not a fourth requirement.
Concrete means a complete solution with input, process and output. Gandhi walking during the Salt Law protest and the Jan Lokpal example illustrate how a champion generates curiosity.
Credibility means people can believe the promise. The lecture's failed Rs 250 phone promise explains why an even cheaper Rs 225 promise would not automatically restore belief.
Identify the champion in the scenario
Ajay has the idea but cannot communicate it well. Sunil believes in it and helps ease resistance, so both contribute without necessarily being the champion.
Jaya has the influence to push the idea through, make people accept it and get it implemented. **Jaya is the champion** in this scenario.
Do not select the first person who thought of the idea merely because they originated it. Look for support-building, resistance-handling and the ability to carry the idea into action.
w3l3: Innovation is a team activity requiring participation and support. Without that, the lecture contrasts structured innovation with ad hoc jugaad.
The four supporting elements are role models, communities of practice, innovation catalysts, and rewards and recognition. They have different jobs, so learn the role of each.
Diverse teams add different perspectives, as illustrated by mixed-background MBA classes. Participation means drawing on these contributions rather than expecting one person to supply everything.
Role models and communities of practice
A role model makes someone think, if they can do it, why not me? External examples are Steve Jobs and Elon Musk; internal colleagues can be more immediate because people see them daily.

A community of practice brings practitioners with a shared interest together to learn and help others. A college coding club is this category, not simply a role model or the generic label team activity.

Other examples are quality circles, scientific associations and IIT robotics or rural-development clubs. The lecture cites computer clubs in discussing the development of products such as iPhone and iPod.
An innovation catalyst encourages idea givers and adds constructive input. The Mughlai-restaurant example is about steering an idea toward what the market needs, not rejecting it without help.
Cash incentives, an Innovator-of-the-Month photograph and a holiday retreat all recognise contributions. The Maruti example combines Rs 100 per idea with inviting idea givers' families.

In the researcher mapping, the professor is a role model, associations/conferences are communities, the PhD supervisor is a catalyst, and publications/promotions provide reward. Match the function each performs.
w3l4: Value creation is the core of economic exchange. A manufacturer converts raw materials into goods, while a college helps a school-leaver become a professional.
The Japanese-practice example separates value-added activity from non-value-added activity. Keep the former and eliminate the latter to improve efficiency.
This distinction prepares the two logics that follow: the question is not only whether value exists, but who creates it and when it is realised.
Goods-dominant logic uses **value-in-exchange**: the firm creates value, manufactures goods and distributes them through the market. Producer and consumer have distinct roles.
Service-dominant logic uses **value-in-use**: value is co-created reciprocally through resources and competences. Producer and consumer roles are not treated as sharply separate.
The manufacturer brings knowledge in production and branding; customers bring knowledge of use and their own lives. Co-creation is mutually beneficial, not a producer-only transfer of finished value.
Co-creation develops value from experiences through engagement platforms. Creativity from customers and employees is at its heart, with meaningful, creative and transformative experiences as the aim.
Lego Ideas is the lecture example, with a community described as one million fans voting on ideas. That number is a lecture-era illustration, not a current membership count.
Co-creation is not necessarily linear, not producer-only and not restricted to services. The lecture also links it to rural development, services and Prahalad's bottom-of-the-pyramid discussion.
w3l5: The two success factors are a backup plan and rapid prototyping. A ready Plan B starts when Plan A fails, like a genset during a power cut, rather than restarting at the idea stage.
Rapid prototyping tests early and responds to shrinking product life cycles. Kishore Biyani's example stresses its importance in what a business attempts.

The Patanjali discussion connects yoga camps with medicines, FMCG and other activities at business-model level. It contrasts maintaining education, yoga, medical and R&D activities in an unfavourable climate with an aggressive swadeshi push in a favourable one.
Measure the process and respect the stakes
Counting new products measures output; counting employees contributing ideas measures part of the process. The lecture prefers a system that measures the process, not final output alone.
Stakes can involve money, brand or life. The aircraft example involves 300 lives; a cricket-final batting-order change shows a different high-stakes setting.
When stakes are high, experiment carefully rather than changing things casually. The need for learning remains, but the consequences determine how cautiously tests must be designed.

Incubation requires a supporting structure and effective review. Examples include higher-education institutes, private institutions, independent public-facing incubators and employee-only company incubators.
The pipeline is submit an idea, review it and incubate it. A weak review outcome can mean rejection or mentorship followed by another review; these are different routes.
Graduation means the venture can stand on its own. Skinner's plant-within-a-plant is a small entity inside a larger plant, another structural example rather than the definition of graduation.
w4l1: A narrow view asks how to do business; the wider view includes developing and co-creating the business. A model explains the way activities, resources and value fit together.
Models may be based on process, marketing, revenue, resources or technology. Walmart is the lecture's logistics-and-marketing example.
Manufacturing or sourcing may sit with one organisation while many others market or support the offering. A model is therefore more than a list of products made by a single factory.
News moves from journalists to stringers, opinion channels and mobile journalism. Transport moves from queues and fixed prices toward pre-booking, live prices and driver location through platforms.
Online retail makes price, size, features and delivery easier to compare. Recorded or virtual education and Kindle illustrate different ways of accessing learning and reading.
The Narayana Hrudayalaya example connects local centres, remote doctors and insurance. These cases show changes in delivery and organisation, not simply a new physical product in each industry.
The business scenario directs the business model, while needs and the way people join or split shape that scenario. Start with the setting and needs instead of assuming one model works everywhere.

Models can also influence business scenarios, so the quiz statement that scenarios may never be directed by models is false. The statement that scenarios are shaped by needs and the way people join or split is true. The relationship is not a one-way rule.
Globalisation, ICT and technological advances are forces shaping the scenario. They help explain why a model suitable for one setting may need to change in another.
Match the company to the model

The lecture pairs Amazon with online retail, Uber with facilitating transport, and Flextronics with manufacturing electronics for many brands. These examples emphasise different roles in a business network.

Amway turns customers into distributors; Netflix illustrates movie rental moving online; Patanjali uses multiple distribution platforms. Treat these as course-era examples, not current company-profile claims.
Grameen Bank is linked with Muhammad Yunus and the Nobel Prize. Keep it distinct from the retail, manufacturing and entertainment examples when matching names to models.
w4l2: Entrepreneur: organise, manage and take risk
An entrepreneur organises and manages a business and takes its risks. In the definition question, entrepreneur is the answer rather than actor, doctor or teacher.
The required qualities include creative, critical and analytical thinking, originality, human relations and communication. **Physical appeal** is not a required entrepreneurial quality in the quiz.
Communication goes beyond the transaction: the LIC example is about customers feeling the company stands by them. It connects relationships to the work of managing a business.
Know the business, not just the fad
Entrepreneurship can bring growth, fame and satisfaction, but it also demands discipline and involves risk. The lecture warns that the entrepreneur may have to bear a fall personally.
Background need not be limiting, but following a fashionable category is not enough. The dot-com bubble and app fad examples ask why this business, rather than something else, is worth pursuing.
Liking doughnuts is not the same as knowing the doughnut business. Separate personal enthusiasm from understanding operations, customers and the risks of the venture.
w4l3: Social entrepreneurship seeks opportunities with a positive impact on a community, society or the world. It develops and funds solutions that directly address social issues such as poverty and problems affecting women or children.

The method combines innovative solutions, capacities, resources and social arrangements to create transformation. It adds an entrepreneurial aspect rather than being defined only by raising philanthropic funds.
Owning a for-profit business alone does not define social entrepreneurship. Look at the purpose and the social problem addressed, not merely whether an organisation sells something.
Course examples of social entrepreneurship include Grameen Bank, Aravind Eye and Aurolab, and Study Hall Foundation. They connect a venture to an identified social need.
The quiz treats eco-friendly products, banking in underserved areas and helping orphaned children as social aims. Mass-producing plastic bottles for profit is the contrasting commercial aim.

ITC and Patanjali are classified as commercial in this course question. Use the stated aim and the course classification rather than assuming any well-known firm automatically counts as a social enterprise.
Divine School is linked with Sudhir educating rag-picking children, and Kailash Satyarthi with the children's cause and Nobel Prize. The shared focus is the people affected, not fame alone.

Other lecture examples include Padman, TDU's copper water purifier, artificial limbs, Amul, Husk Power and Narayana Hrudayalaya. Keep each in the social-problem discussion instead of treating the names as definitions.
The rural-women scheme connects trade training, tools and seed money to making carpets, clothes or food, then to showrooms. It illustrates skills, resources and access to a market working together.
w4l4: From crowded markets to blue oceans
A red ocean is an existing market dominated by competition. A blue ocean seeks uncontested space and new demand rather than competing only within existing boundaries.

The six paths look across alternative industries, strategic groups, the chain of buyers, complementary offerings, functional or emotional appeal, and time. These are ways to reconstruct market boundaries.
**Looking across space** is not one of the six paths. Do not replace time or another named path with a word that merely sounds like a boundary.
Across industries, the lecture uses NetJets' fractional jet ownership, NTT DoCoMo's mobile internet, FabIndia and Gandhi Ashram. The path asks where alternatives satisfy a related need.
Across strategic groups, the examples are Lexus, Curves and Patanjali. Keep this grouping distinct from changing which buyer the offer addresses.

Across the chain of buyers, examples include Novo Nordisk's Novo Pen, Crocin, Scholastic books and Kindle. Learn the path alongside its examples rather than memorising one undifferentiated company list.
Complementary offerings consider what surrounds the core service. In education, the lecture includes infrastructure, ambience and laptops, not the teaching product in isolation.
Across functional or emotional appeal, the examples include Swatch, Cemex selling a dream and ACC construction advice. This path changes the basis of the appeal.
Across time, the lecture mentions the European Union and Apple's downloadable music. Time is the named path; space is the distractor in the six-path question.
Visualise the strategy in four steps
The principle is to focus on the big picture rather than only numbers. The four steps are visual awakening, visual exploration, visual strategy fair and visual communication.
Awakening notices differences and change; exploration uses field visits; the strategy fair includes a world-café exercise; communication shares the result among peers.

Reflex path, strategy process and marketing mix are other labels, not this four-step list. Daniel Kahneman's book mentioned in the lecture is **Thinking, Fast and Slow**, not Start, Grow, and Run, The Innovator's Dilemma or Zero to One.
Blue-ocean thinking looks beyond existing demand toward non-customers and the biggest catchment. It does not mean only taking a larger share of the same buyers.
The lecture examples include Callaway Golf, Activa for elderly people, women and students, Cadbury's Kuch Meetha Ho Jaye, multiplexes and Spencer's. Tooth whitening and amla juice are further cases.
Keep the two tools apart: six paths reconstruct boundaries; four visual steps help see and communicate strategy. Both support finding new demand beyond a crowded red ocean.
w4l5: A strategy needs focus and divergence
w4c59
w4c60
A strong strategy has focus, divergence and a compelling tagline. Focus directs attention; divergence keeps the offer from simply copying the prevailing pattern.
A tagline helps people recognise the promise, as in the LIC Jeevan Anand recall example. It belongs with the strategy rather than being an unrelated slogan exercise.
These three qualities are not the four actions. Keep the three strategy qualities separate from Eliminate, Reduce, Raise and Create.
The four actions: ERRC
w4c61
w4c62
The Four Actions Framework is **Eliminate, Reduce, Raise and Create**. It asks which parts of an offering should disappear, become smaller, become stronger or be introduced.
When Eliminate and Create are already supplied, the missing pair is **Reduce and Raise**. That exact pair is what the quiz tests.
Reuse, Recycle and Recreate are distractors, not replacements for the framework's names. Do not substitute another familiar four-word environmental or design list.
Cirque du Soleil: apply each action
w4c63
w4c64
w4c65
w4c66
Cirque du Soleil eliminated star performers, animal shows, aisle concessions and multiple arenas. The lecture compares its approach with Ringling Brothers and smaller regional circuses.
It reduced fun and humour and thrills and danger, while raising the uniqueness of the venue. Keep reduce and raise attached to the right attributes.

It created themes, a refined viewing environment, multiple productions, and artistic music and dance. These additions explain why its new offer was not simply a cheaper version of a conventional circus.
Use a strategy canvas without copying a case
w4c67
w4c68
w4c69
w4c70
Further ERRC examples include Scorpio, Narayana Hrudayalaya, Patanjali, Tata Ace and Magic, Maruti, and television serials. They show that the framework can be applied beyond a circus.

The lecture includes separate strategy canvases for Patanjali Ayurveda, DoMS IIT Roorkee and bio-residue energy. A canvas compares the choices in a particular offering rather than prescribing one universal list of features.
Review the named tools accurately: strong strategy means focus, divergence and tagline; ERRC means eliminate, reduce, raise and create. For the missing pair, retain reduce and raise.
w5l1: The AMA definition used in the lecture describes creating, communicating, delivering and exchanging offerings that have value. The audiences are customers, clients, partners and society at large.
Marketing needs commitment and intensity of effort, not simply an invention waiting to sell itself. Marketing of innovation means commercialising a novel offering.
Marketing and innovation also includes innovating marketing itself. Keep the offering being marketed separate from changes in the way it is communicated or delivered.
Examples: the offering and its delivery
The health ladder moves from treating walk-in patients to finding patients and then bringing lower-cost solutions to their doorstep through technology. It illustrates a changing delivery model.

LIFX is the mobile-app-controlled bulb; Mitticool is the mud refrigerator praised by Kalam; Amul illustrates integrated communication. Each name is attached to a particular feature or marketing point.

The lecture's wider firm list includes Apple, Google, Toyota, GE, Microsoft, P&G, 3M, Disney, Sony, Honda, BMW, Samsung, Walmart, Starbucks and Patanjali. It is a set of examples, not a current ranking.
w5l2: From science to socially usable technology
w5c12
w5c13
w5c14
w5c15
w5c25
The course sequence is **Science, Engineering, Technology**. Science supplies fundamental principles; engineering applies them to design; technology produces usable impact and wealth.
A scientific invention is a new idea from R&D. Technological innovation transforms an invention into a socially usable product, so not every scientific invention becomes an innovation.

The radio example links Faraday, Maxwell and Hertz with science, Marconi with radio from 1896, and transatlantic wireless signals with December 1901. It illustrates the sequence rather than reversing technology and engineering.
What the technological innovation process includes
w5c16
w5c17
w5c18
w5c19
w5c20
w5c24

Technological innovation is complex, involving technological, social and economic factors. It can require substantial investment and take decades; the quiz rejects describing it merely as a new use of existing technology.

For Week 5 Q4, the keyed set is **basic research, product development, co-creation, scaling up and experimentation: a, b, d, f, h**. Do not add societal impact, excluding existing knowledge or trial and error to that answer set.

That keyed selection is narrower than the lecture's broader discussion: societal impact can be positive or negative, with the Blue Whale game used as a negative example. Do not read the quiz selection as a claim that impact never exists.
Bright's eight stages: idea to demonstration
w5c21
Stage 1 is initiation from a discovery or market need. Stage 2 is synthesis using existing knowledge and trial and error.
Stage 3 verifies the theory or design. Stage 4 demonstrates it in the laboratory through a breadboard model.
These stages explain the early development route. Existing knowledge and trial and error appear in this lecture framework even though the separate Q4 answer set does not select them.
Bright's eight stages: introduction to proliferation
w5c22
w5c23
Stage 5 explores alternatives through prototypes and field trials; Stage 6 is commercial introduction. The product must move beyond laboratory demonstration.
Stage 7 is widespread adoption, including cash flows and societal impact. Stage 8 is proliferation into new markets.
Microwave technology reaching cooking ovens and aircraft radar reaching speed enforcement illustrate proliferation. New markets come after introduction and adoption in this sequence.
w5l3: Match the four types of innovation
The four types are radical, micro-radical, generational and incremental. Radical innovation is revolutionary and can create an industry; the quiz pairs it with creation of the World Wide Web.

The other quiz matches are micro-radical with virtual trial rooms, generational with 3G-to-4G networks, and incremental with smartphone-camera enhancement. Micro-radical and generational innovation build on existing capabilities.

Other radical examples include flying machines, Watt's steam engine and supercomputers. Windows/iPhone versions illustrate generations, while higher car mileage illustrates incremental performance improvement or cost reduction.
Use an S-curve with the right planning horizon

An S-curve moves through a slow start, rapid growth and maturity. It helps stakeholders anticipate a technology's trajectory and plan for future challenges. On the diagram, time runs horizontally and technology performance rises vertically toward an upper limit L.
Incremental innovation involves short-term planning, while micro-radical and generational innovation involve longer-term planning. Do not reverse these horizons in the statement question.
Radical innovations are rare and difficult to plan from an S-curve. The curve supports anticipation, not a guarantee of when an entirely new breakthrough will occur.
The lecture contrasts first/second-generation R&D, treated as an expense and left to itself, with third-generation R&D embedded in corporate and business planning.
The Week 5 key rejects the statement that India mostly has third-generation companies. Treat this as the lecture's classification, not a freshly measured description of Indian firms today.

Planning forecasts technology and market needs, disaggregates them through a technology-market matrix, and formulates an innovation mission. The identity examples pair 3M with coatings, Canon with optical imaging, Honda with engines/power trains, NEC with VLSI/systems integration and DuPont with chemistry.
w5l4: Base, key, pacing and emerging technology
**Base** technology is ageing and widely known, so its widespread use does not provide competitive advantage. **Key** technology is embodied in products and differentiates the company.
**Pacing** technology has demonstrated its ability to change competition and is moving into development. **Emerging** technology is still in early research, with unknown but promising potential.
For the matching question this is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv. Do not confuse pacing, whose competitive effect has been demonstrated, with emerging technology whose potential is still unknown.
The technology lifecycle moves from emergence through growth and maturity to decline. The lecture uses early electric cars, Kodak film and the move from wired telephones to mobile as illustrations.
A technology audit considers present SWOT across core technologies, products, markets and competition, then future SWOT to formulate a technology plan.
Timing strategies form a continuum and may be combined. The lifecycle stage or audit does not force every firm into one permanently exclusive strategy.
Offensive strategy aims to be a first mover, illustrated by IBM, TI and DuPont. It is not defined as merely maintaining the status quo.
Defensive strategy follows the leader. Counter-offensive strategy responds to the leader's dominance rather than simply accepting its position.
Keep the direction of action clear: lead, follow, or counter the leader. Those are different choices even when a firm combines strategies over time.
Imitative strategy is intensive in design, production and service, not research. Applications engineering develops and designs using existing technology.
Dependent strategy resembles a branch plant focused on production and marketing. The quiz rejects describing it as developing core strategy with the parent company.
**Absorbent strategy acquires a licence to exploit innovation in the domestic market.** That is the true statement in the strategy question; retain the licensing and home-market elements together.
w5l5: The lecture describes forecasting as over a century old, with expansion after World War II and horizons of 3-25 years or more. It is multidisciplinary rather than confined to one technical specialty.
Monitoring watches for signals of change, using sources such as New Scientist and Scientific American. The NTPC plant-load-factor example explains why past performance alone is not enough.
Forecasting anticipates developments, trends and threats and supports R&D, investment and strategic planning. Both statements in the final quiz question are true.

The course-key tools are morphological analysis, Delphi, the Pearl function based on the S-curve, and envelope curve with trend extrapolation: **b, c, e, f**. Time-series analysis and moving average are not selected in this question.
Pearl describes an S-curve with an upper limit L; Gompertz is another S-curve function. An envelope curve is formed by successive technologies, not by assuming one technology improves forever.
The lecture's trend examples are light-source efficiency since 1850 and combat-aircraft speed since 1909. These illustrate trajectories, not a promise that extrapolation predicts every breakthrough.
Delphi: choose the expert panel carefully
Delphi invites experts and proceeds iteratively. It uses their judgments to explore technological futures rather than relying only on a plotted historical trend.
Selecting the right panel members is the key issue highlighted in the lecture. An iterative process cannot compensate for asking people without relevant expertise.
Remember Delphi as the expert-panel technique in the forecasting-tool list. Do not confuse it with morphological analysis, which combines parts of a solution.
Morphological analysis systematically explores combinations of sub-capabilities. Break a problem into dimensions, list alternatives for each, then examine combinations.
For bricks, dimensions include material, forming, bonding, properties and shape. Examples span clay/metal/plastic/waste, extrusion/moulding/pressing, and heat/chemical/molecular bonding.

Opacity, insulation, elasticity and aesthetics are properties; rectangular, spherical, interlocking and cubical are forms. Fly ash is the waste-material option used for bricks, not a forming or bonding method.
w6l1: Sustainability as a shared, long-term problem
w6c1
w6c4
w6c5

The lecture connects sustainability with generations, the Ganges, public-interest litigation and thinking big. Its practical message is to build progress bit by bit rather than expect one isolated gesture to solve everything.
The Ganges example refers to 500 million people linked to the river and a project team of about 110 people across eight IITs. Those are lecture figures, not a new census or current staffing report.
Chennai and Kedarnath floods are discussed as avoidable-disaster examples. Keep the concern with social and environmental consequences together with the need for organised action.
Sustainable innovations: what changes
w6c2
w6c3
Film farming is described as using no soil and one-tenth of the water. Reusable cardboard packaging gives directions for turning it into something else; wood stoves turn waste heat into electricity.

The lecture also presents airborne windmills with a 50%-more-energy claim, carbon-neutral plastic, e-waste kiosks and an ethical smartphone. These are the course's examples and claimed benefits, not independently updated product specifications.
The common idea is to change resource use, waste or social effects through an offering. Identify the specific change rather than treating the word sustainable as an explanation by itself.
Societal development and the quiz examples
w6c6
w6c7
w6c8
w6c9
w6c10

The societal-development example is **Narmada ji ka Safai Abhiyan**, linked in the lecture with Shantikunj, Haridwar. Hospital businesses or a coal-powered cutter are not the answer to that specific example question.

Vivekanand Needam combines greening barren land, hollow bricks for indoor temperature, plastic-bottle drip irrigation and bacterial treatment of human waste. Several linked practices contribute rather than one decorative green label.
For sustainable-innovation examples, **both Aravind Eye Care and Narayana Hrudayalaya count**. Selecting only one leaves the course-key answer incomplete.
w6l2: The five actors are government, corporates, individuals, academia and media. The lecture asks them to contribute together rather than assigning the whole responsibility to one actor.
Supporting conditions include resource allocation, culture, directing attention and developing belief. Resources alone are not the whole set of conditions.
Keep the actor list apart from the condition list: academia is an actor; culture is a condition. This helps identify what a question is asking you to classify.

The lecture calls for directing attention from youth's self-opulence, elders' retirement and voluntary unemployment toward constructive involvement. It also stresses reducing criticism and scepticism while developing belief.
The sugar-industry example links sugar, electricity, alcohol and by-products. Singapore is used as the sustainability-culture example.

Academia's pedal-rickshaw efficiency project illustrates a practical contribution. Keep the improvement being investigated with the actor, instead of treating the rickshaw itself as a definition of sustainability.
w6l3: Rubenstein's wording covers new and improved **products, processes, materials and services**. These are the four spans to remember together.
The definition includes transferring them to a plant or market where they are appropriate. Development alone is not the entire wording.
In the attribution question, keep this wording with Rubenstein. Shorter alternatives such as goods and services, or idea, method and device, are not the specific phrasing tested.
Category 1 combines a new product/process with an old use or problem; Category 2 is old product/process and old use. The lecture gives new medication and just-in-time for 1, and a stapler for 2.
Category 3 is new product/process and new use. **Bar codes belong to Category 3**, not categories 1, 2 or 4.
Category 4 applies an old product/process to a new use, illustrated by Listerine. Track both axes, because noticing only a new use is not enough to distinguish 3 from 4.

The random or Schumpeterian school centres on entrepreneurs, entrepreneurial risk, trial and error, and learning from failures. It also discusses organisational DNA/culture and experimental units or spin-offs.
The systematic or value-innovation school uses patterns, ways of thinking, theory, methodologies and frameworks. Its aim is to maximise opportunity while minimising risk.

Jaws Polymers pioneering PET jars and later losing the market is the random-school example. Keep the two schools distinct rather than assuming every planned framework is trial-and-error entrepreneurship.
w6l4: Enterprise size: use the course-era limits

Innovation matters for success at any enterprise size. For this course, learn the investment limits shown in the lecture; these are historical course figures, not advice about current MSME registration law.

Manufacturing plant-and-machinery limits are micro up to Rs 25 lakh, small up to Rs 5 crore, medium up to Rs 10 crore, and large above Rs 10 crore. The quiz's medium limit is Rs 10 crore, also Rs 100 million.
Services use equipment limits: micro Rs 10 lakh, small Rs 2 crore and medium Rs 5 crore. Do not substitute the service-micro figure for the manufacturing-micro figure.

For the assignment, ASPIRE expands to **A Scheme for Promoting Innovation and Rural Entrepreneurship**. The government scheme name is A Scheme for Promotion of Innovation, Rural Industries and Entrepreneurship. Its Livelihood Business Incubators are abbreviated LBI.
The lecture lists NSIC, KVIC and the Coir Board as supporting bodies and places the first LBI in Uttar Pradesh. Keep the programme, incubator type and supporting organisations distinct.

KVIC is **Khadi and Village Industries Commission**. The assignment key instead accepts the option Khadi and Village Industries Committee. Remember the keyed wording for that question without learning Committee as the actual name.
Economic benefits include reduced expenses, higher productivity from modernised tools, meeting demand for eco-responsible personalised products, and diversification through sustainability consulting.

Social initiatives improve working conditions, for example less dust through automated waste recovery or reduced noise through soundproof roofing. A girl-child-friendly school belongs to the social category.

Classify the benefit being described: lower expenses and meeting demand are economic, while conditions for workers or people are social. They are not interchangeable simply because one project can help both.
Environmental initiatives cut impacts at source, such as recovering paper waste, and use eco-designed or recyclable materials. Reforestation can protect local biodiversity.
The keyed benefits are reducing impact at source and protecting biodiversity. **Exploiting local biodiversity and using single-use plastic are not benefits** in this comparison.

Keep the three dimensions together: economic concerns costs and demand, social concerns people, environmental concerns materials and ecological impact. Read the actual benefit before selecting its category.
w6l5: Gary Klein and the five Cs
The five Cs of insight are associated with **Gary Klein**, author of Seeing What Others Don't. Rubenstein is the innovation-definition attribution, not the five-Cs answer.
The five are connections, contradictions, creative desperation, coincidences and curiosities. Do not combine the last two into one term and accidentally lose a C.
The lecture gives different examples and levels of reliability for these routes. Learn the route with the example, rather than assuming every surprising event produces a sound insight.
The lecture reports connections in 80% of 120 insights. Its Pearl Harbour example links Japanese learning from an Italy-Britain battle to a later application.

Contradictions appear in nearly 40% in the lecture account. Paulson and Pellegrini comparing beliefs with house prices, and Einstein's space-time work, illustrate noticing something that does not fit.

These percentages describe routes in the cited set of insights, not mutually exclusive portions that must add to 100%. Keep connections and contradictions distinct without forcing them into a pie chart.
Creative desperation is illustrated by firefighters setting another fire to make an escape. The lecture contrasts necessity as the mother of invention with desperation as the father of insight.

Gottlieb's symptom coincidences leading to AIDS recognition illustrate coincidences; Fleming observing bacteria dying near mould illustrates curiosity and penicillin. These are different routes even though both involve noticing a pattern.

The lecture cautions that coincidences and curiosities account for only 10% and can mislead. Indian cases mentioned include Narayana Hrudayalaya, Husk Power, Veena Vadini, Digital Diaries and Trans Disciplinary University.
w7l1: Intellectual capital is knowledge usable to create wealth, including employee knowledge and skills. The lecture describes it as what remains after tangible assets are stripped away.
It includes processes, designs, inventions, customer and supplier relationships, software, manuals and databases. It is broader than registered patents.
The creation sequence is **Purpose, Strategy, Information, Knowledge**. Purpose and strategy determine what information is needed before that information becomes useful knowledge.

Intellectual assets are the identified, documented and shareable part of intellectual capital. Customer relationships are capital, but do not become an asset in this framework until identified and documented.

Intellectual property is the legally protected part of those assets. The sequence is **Intellectual Capital, Intellectual Assets, Intellectual Property**; patents, knowledge economy or ownership do not replace the last stage.

The management process searches, identifies, captures, documents, indexes, stores, augments and replicates knowledge. The lecture distinguishes employees, whom the firm does not own, from assets created in the organisation.
The two families of intellectual property
WIPO's definition concerns creations of the mind used in commerce. The lecture groups intellectual property into industrial property and copyright.
Industrial property includes patents, trademarks, designs and geographical indications. Copyright covers literary works, films, music, art and architecture.
These are broad families rather than a claim that IP means patents alone. Keep the family names separate from individual rights such as a trademark or patent.
w7l2: IPRs let owners benefit from inventions and creative works. The lecture links them with Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the Paris Convention of 1883 and Berne Convention of 1886, both administered by WIPO.

Protection is presented as encouraging resources for innovation, jobs, new industries and quality of life. WIPO's balance is between **innovators and the public**, not a pair built around industry or the economy.
Patents are one type of IPR, not the whole set. Copyright supports creative sectors, patents incentivise products, and trademarks support confidence and action against counterfeiting.
Patents: application, term and granting route

A patent is an exclusive right to an invention, generally for a limited 20-year term in the course account. National or regional offices grant patents; the lecture names EPO and OAPI as regional examples.
The application includes a title, technical field, background, description, drawings and claims. Claims define the extent of protection, while the description explains the invention.

PCT means Patent Cooperation Treaty, administered by WIPO. One international application supports seeking protection in multiple countries; do not mistake the application route for a single automatically granted worldwide patent.
The lecture lists three requirements for a mark: it should be distinctive, not misleading and not similar to an existing mark. These concern recognising the source of an offering.
Distinctiveness separates the mark from generic wording. Avoid treating any ordinary product name as automatically protectable merely because a business uses it.
This is course-level revision, not clearance for a real registration. An actual mark and jurisdiction would need a current assessment rather than relying on this short list.
w7l3: The broad groups are industrial property and copyright; the three prominent rights are patents, copyrights and trademarks. IP protection is wider than those three names alone.

The lecture also lists trade secrets and know-how, industrial design, geographical indications and integrated-circuit layout design, with non-competition and non-disclosure agreements as supporting tools.
A luxury-car exterior, a soft-drink recipe and Darjeeling Tea illustrate industrial design, trade secret and GI respectively. In the quiz, all three fall within the IPR discussion.
Patent: what it protects and where

The lecture describes a patent as enabling the holder to prevent others making, using, selling, offering or importing the protected invention. It is not simply ownership of an idea without defined protection.
Patent protection is territorial: it operates within the geographical boundary where protection applies. Do not infer worldwide coverage from the word patent alone.
The course's patentability requirements are **novel, nonobvious and useful**. Remember all three rather than substituting a business's popularity or commercial size.

Trademarks distinguish source through brand names or distinctive appearance, including product/packaging shape, colour and texture. Google, IBM, Apple and Microsoft are the lecture examples; generic terms are not protectable in this account.

The lecture describes trademark life as potentially perpetual and says registration is not always legally required. Treat this as course recall, not a claim that a real mark never needs renewal or jurisdiction-specific checks.

A geographical indication links quality or distinctiveness to origin, illustrated by Darjeeling Tea. Misleading use is the issue; the lecture lists injunctions, damages, fines and imprisonment among possible sanctions.
Copyright, trade secrets and matching rights
Copyright protects the expression of an idea, **not the idea itself**. A novelist's manuscript is the copyright example in the matching question.

Trade-secret examples include a chemical formula, manufacturing process, machine design or business model; Coca-Cola's formula is the lecture illustration. Secrecy is distinct from disclosing an invention through a patent application.

Match a medicine's exclusive patent right with patent, and a Nike logo or brand name with trademark. Do not confuse a logo's source-identifying function with the general copyright rule about expression.
w7l4: The lecture presents the patent system's objective as encouraging technology and industry development, not promoting monopolies as an end in themselves. Exclusive rights can encourage research, disclosure and investment.
Disclosure contrasts with retaining a trade secret; reward helps address development expenses and investment in production lines. Keep the incentive and disclosure purposes together.

For India, the course names the 1959 Ayyangar Committee report as a base, then 1911 legislation, the Patents Act 1970 in force from 1972, and amendments in 1999, 2002 and 2005. This is the lecture's historical timeline, not a complete current-law guide.
Patent process and disclosure before filing
The lecture's process lists filing, priority date, publication, examination, the Controller, pre-grant opposition, and grant or refusal. Filing is not the same event as receiving a granted right.

In the assignment scenario, the seminar is treated as a public disclosure before filing that defeats novelty, so the key chooses the no-protection option. This is a course answer, not a universal ruling that every seminar removes every form of IP protection.

The important order is disclosure **before filing**, not simply before a patent is granted. Actual patent law can allow exceptions or grace periods; other rights must be assessed separately. The inventor's home region alone does not define the territory of patent protection.
Copyright is automatic, expression is protected
The lecture describes copyright in original works as automatic, without mandatory registration or a copyright symbol. Optional registration can help prove ownership.
Rights include use, reproduction, distribution, performance and display. The protected subject is the expression in the work, not the underlying idea itself.
For the quiz, reject the statement that copyright protects an idea as such. Keep that distinction separate from a patent's novelty requirement and the historical patent-system timeline.
w7l5: Bajaj versus TVS: patent and interim order

The Bajaj-TVS dispute concerns a patent and twin-spark technology: Bajaj DTSi and TVS CCVTi in the lecture. Bajaj's cited patent is No. 195904, with priority dated 16 July 2002 and a stated 20-year term.
The 2009 Supreme Court order discussed allowed TVS sales with a receiver checking accounts. It did not decide the merits of the patent claim in that interim account.
Distinguish permission to sell under conditions from a final ruling that a patent is valid or infringed. The case must not be reduced to a winner label without the order's limitation.
This is the **Maaza trademark** case, not the twin-spark patent dispute. The lecture says Bisleri sold the Indian rights to Coca-Cola.
The ruling discussed treats export as a sale, so exporting from India can infringe the transferred mark. Territorial rights and the place of export matter in the case account.
The Delhi High Court injunction barred use in India and export in the lecture's account. Learn these as the historical case facts, not a statement about current unrelated beverage rights.
Ericsson's case concerns eight standard-essential patents. Xiaomi relied on a Qualcomm-chip licensing claim, which differs from claiming that every Xiaomi device could be sold without conditions.
The Delhi High Court allowed sales on conditions in the lecture account: Qualcomm-chip devices only, with Rs 100 per device deposited as royalty.
Keep the three cases apart: Bajaj-TVS is twin-spark patent technology; Coca-Cola-Bisleri is Maaza trademark; Ericsson-Xiaomi is standard-essential patents and conditional sales.
w8l1: A model covers the whole value flow
A business model explains how a business **creates, delivers and captures value**. Learn the whole flow rather than selecting only one part of it.

A value proposition and a revenue model are parts of the business model, not synonyms for the complete model. The proposition concerns the value offered; the whole model must also explain delivery and capture.
Start by knowing the business, the organisation, capabilities and capacities, customers and resources. What business are we in and who are we are different questions that both inform the model.
Components and non-components in the quiz
The lecture's components are target customers, value proposition, revenue streams and costs, key activities, and channels. Channels cover promotion and distribution.
Competition, government regulations, and review and feedback are not selected as components in this course question. They can affect a business without becoming items in the named component list.

The lecture applies models to heavy electricals, MDH or a salt producer, construction, hospitals, forest bio-residue and automotive manufacturing. Use the same component questions across those different examples.
w8l2: Two reasons a business model fails
A model can fail because one of its elements does not work as intended. Ask whether the element meets expectations and operates to its potential.
It can also fail because it cannot adapt to the changing environment or competitive landscape. A previously workable model is not guaranteed to remain workable.
The lecture lists Nano as a failure example. The useful distinction is internal element performance versus failure to adapt, not a claim that every failure has one identical cause.
Remedies: anticipate, diagnose and match capacity
A futuristic approach anticipates what features customers will want in a product, service or process. It addresses change before simply repeating the old offer.
Diagnose symptoms to find and eliminate the cause, considering alternatives. Also match capacities and capabilities with the value proposition, so the business can deliver what it promises.

All three are remedies in the quiz. Royal Enfield, Bata, management education and forest bio-residue are lecture examples used in the failure-and-turnaround discussion, not reasons to select only one remedy.
w8l3: Entrepreneurship is the chain of creating, developing and managing a venture: recognising opportunities, taking calculated risks and generating value. The lecture links Schumpeter with its role in economic development.
The process includes opportunity recognition and resource acquisition. **Pre-founding** identifies and evaluates the opportunity; **founding** involves planning, resources, incorporation and entry.
**Early development** builds the company and penetrates the market. Keep these in sequence rather than moving incorporation into pre-founding or market penetration before the venture is founded.
Incubation is the support process; an incubator is the organisation and infrastructure providing it. A startup incubator is a collaborative programme intended to help new ventures succeed.

Support can include workspace, seed funding, mentoring and training. Incubators are described as usually non-profit and run by public or private entities, with university links including IITs, NITs and IIMs.

The goal is viable, freestanding firms that leave the programme. The assignment accepts **a year or two**, while the lecture describes roughly 2-3 years. The shared principle is time-limited support, not weeks, decades, indefinite support or hand-holding through the whole business journey.
Features and services of an incubator
Core features are networking, shared resources, mentorship and access to experts. A sole focus on established companies is not a feature in the quiz.

Services include business basics, marketing, accounting, finance, help with bank loans and guarantees, and access to angels or venture capital. These support early-stage development rather than replacing the entrepreneur.
Strategic partners, IP and legal counsel, and regulatory-compliance help are further services. Match the service to a need while keeping the exit goal of an independent firm in view.

Business incubators support regional growth and employment through business development, focusing on early-stage growth-oriented ventures. The third-generation International Enterprise Centre example emphasises knowledge-based business and broad support.

Technology incubators help complete technology development and promote technology firms. They are often linked with universities, R&D institutes or science and technology parks, supporting transfer and diffusion.

Technology Innovation Centres connect R&D and commercialisation. TBI means **Technology Business Incubator**, focused on technology- or knowledge-intensive firms with academic links; it is not merely another name for any established company.
w8l4: Initial funding, angels and venture capital

A startup needs initial and working capital. The lecture names self-funding first, followed by incubators and other finance. The assignment nevertheless keys **angel investors** as its primary early-stage source. Keep that specific key separate from a universal claim about all startups.
An angel is an affluent individual supplying startup capital in return for debt or equity. Business angel, informal investor, angel funder and seed investor are the related names listed.

Venture capital funds startups or expansion while seeking a large return. Keep that institutional funding role distinct from the individual angel and from a later loan. Government grants, IPOs and Self are not the choices accepted by this assignment key. That rejection is specific to this question, not a claim that self-funding or grants never support new ventures.
Debt is a loan against collateral such as assets, receivables or intellectual property. The quiz accepts that **IP can be collateral**; do not exclude it merely because it is intangible.

The venture-debt discussion concerns startups lacking the assets needed for traditional loans. In this course sequence it follows VC equity, so the claim that debt is the first level of funding is false.
The lecture mentions an equity option if repayment is late, stated as 10%-15% of the debt amount. These are lecture terms, not a universal contract or a live financing offer.
Venture debt: remember the course terms
The lecture presents venture debt after VC funding as a way to fund growth while avoiding immediate dilution. Its figures are up to 25% of the venture-equity round and a 24-36 month repayment term.
Named fund examples are Unicorn India at Rs 600 crore, IvyCap Ventures at Rs 500 crore and Alteria Capital at Rs 1,000 crore. These are historical lecture figures rather than current fund sizes.

Hari Menon's Big Basket example uses venture debt for capital expenditure. Review the distinctions: angels for early funding, collateral including IP for debt, and equity before venture debt in this course account.
w8l5: Use needs and resources to find future markets
The future-market lens begins with needs, available resources and the place of innovation in meeting those needs. A market opportunity is not defined by a fashionable technology alone.
The lecture discusses education, energy, the economy and food security, then disasters, defence and housing. These are areas to investigate rather than a single prescribed business model.

Read these broad areas alongside the official nine-area question that follows. Some broad labels are expressed more specifically in the answer list, such as housing through urbanisation and smart cities.
The official question selects all nine areas
The first four areas are technology and digital innovation, renewable energy and sustainability, healthcare and biotechnology, and agriculture and food security. Keep each paired description intact.
The next four are disaster management, educational technology, fintech and financial inclusion, and urbanisation and smart cities. **Defence** is the ninth area.
The course-key answer includes **all nine**, not only the most familiar sectors. When the question lists them together, do not omit defence or choose a partial set.
